extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and instructors in real analysis / measure theory and Fourier analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and precise conditions connecting Stieltjes measures and their distribution functions, integration-by-parts with Stieltjes measures, functions of bounded variation, and Fourier-series results (Riesz–Fischer, Dirichlet–Jordan) as presented in a measure-theory textbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness theorem for Fourier coefficients (Corollary 6.50)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is in L1 and has all Fourier coefficients 0, then f is the 0 element in L1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: convolve f with the Fejér kernels K_N to obtain K_N * f whose Fourier coefficients are cn(K_N) cn(f) = 0; K_N * f is continuous and tends to f in L1, hence f = 0. (Uses Propositions 6.47, 6.18 and Theorem 6.48.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Riesz–Fischer Theorem (Theorem 6.51)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a doubly infinite sequence of complex numbers {c_n} with ∑_{n=-∞}^{∞} |c_n|^2 < ∞, there exists an f in L2 whose Fourier series is ∑ c_n e^{inx}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: define partial sums f_N(x)=∑_{|n|≤N} c_n e^{inx}; by Parseval these partial sums form a Cauchy sequence in L2 and hence converge in L2 to some f. Continuity of the inner product yields that the Fourier coefficients of the limit equal the given c_n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Stieltjes measure and distribution function
rubrics_metrics.description: A Stieltjes measure is a Borel measure on R. Given a Stieltjes measure µ, associate the function F (the distribution function) defined (in the text) by piecewise formulas so that F records cumulative mass relative to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key properties of the associated distribution function F: (i) F is nondecreasing, (ii) F is continuous from the right (i.e., lim_{x↓x0} F(x)=F(x0)), and (iii) F(0)=0. The measure µ is completely determined by its distribution function via µ((a,b]) = F(b) - F(a) (with appropriate one-sided limits when endpoints are included).

rubrics_metrics.name: One-to-one correspondence: Stieltjes measures ↔ monotone right-continuous functions (Theorem 6.52)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stieltjes measures µ stand in one-one correspondence with functions F:R→R satisfying (i) F nondecreasing, (ii) F continuous from the right, and (iii) F(0)=0; F is the distribution function of µ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction of µ from F: define µ on bounded intervals by µ((a,b]) = F(b) - F(a) (and analogous formulas for other endpoint conventions using one-sided limits), extend additively to the ring of finite disjoint unions of bounded intervals, verify regularity and complete additivity (imitating Lebesgue-measure construction), and then extend to Borel σ-algebra. Show distribution function of constructed µ equals F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point masses and jumps of distribution function
rubrics_metrics.description: A point mass at p of weight µ({p}) corresponds to a jump of size µ({p}) in the distribution function F at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: F that is 0 for x<0 and 1 for x≥0 corresponds to the delta measure at 0. More generally, if µ has a point mass at p of weight w>0, then F has a jump of magnitude w at p; µ can be decomposed into point masses plus a measure with no point masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of purely singular continuous Stieltjes measures (Cantor example)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist nonzero Stieltjes measures carried on sets of Lebesgue measure 0 whose distribution functions are continuous (Cantor function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Construct approximating monotone continuous functions Fn constant on the complementary open intervals of the Cantor set with suitable step sizes so that Fn converges uniformly to a continuous nondecreasing limit F; the associated measure µ is supported on the Cantor set, assigns 0 to singletons, and µ([0,1]
C)=0 while µ(C)>0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration by parts with Stieltjes measures (Theorem 6.53)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a<b, F monotone increasing and continuous from the right at a and b, µ the associated Stieltjes measure. If G is C1 on [a,b] with derivative g, then ∫_a^b F(x) g(x) dx = G(b)F(b) - G(a)F(a) - ∫_{(a,b]} G dµ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to the case where F is the distribution function of µ; use partitions and mean-value theorem, estimate differences, choose partition mesh small via uniform continuity of G and g, and pass to the limit. The theorem allows integration-by-parts formulas where the 'derivative' of F is replaced by the Stieltjes measure µ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of bounded variation and basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A real-valued function f on [a,b] is of bounded variation if there exists M such that for every partition a=x0< x1<...<xn=b one has ∑_{i=1}^n |f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})| ≤ M. The least such M is the BV 'norm' k f k_{BV}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: arbitrary bounded monotone functions and any function with continuous derivative are of bounded variation. The only functions with k·k_{BV}=0 are constants. Every function of bounded variation has left and right limits at each point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive and negative variations and Jordan decomposition (Proposition 6.54)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f of bounded variation, define V^+(f)(x) and V^-(f)(x) as supremums of certain partial sums over partitions of [a,x]; these are monotone increasing and satisfy f(x)-f(a)=V^+(f)(x)-V^-(f)(x). Hence f is the difference of two monotone increasing functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definitions provide a canonical Jordan decomposition; consequences include that V^+ and V^- inherit monotonicity and one-sided continuity properties, and that BV functions can be treated via monotone-function techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dirichlet–Jordan Theorem for Fourier series (Theorem 6.55)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is a function of bounded variation on [-π,π], then the Fourier series of f converges at each point to the appropriate value (the text indicates the usual midpoint/one-sided average) and it converges uniformly to f(x) on any compact set on which the periodic extension of f is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: decompose f via Jordan decomposition into monotone increasing parts; extend these to R by constants outside the interval; associate Stieltjes measures and apply integration by parts to relate Fourier coefficients of f to Fourier–Stieltjes coefficients of the measure; use Fejér's theorem and a Tauberian theorem (Proposition 1.50) to get pointwise convergence from boundedness of n c_n, which follows from estimates on coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier–Stieltjes series and boundedness of coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Borel measure µ on an interval treated as periodic, define Fourier–Stieltjes coefficients c_n = ∫ e^{-inx} dµ(x); then the Fourier–Stieltjes coefficients are bounded, with |c_n| ≤ µ((−π,π]) (or analogous total mass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: to avoid endpoint point-mass complications one may shift the interval by choosing c so endpoints carry no point masses; periodic identification or matching point masses at endpoints is suggested when forming a periodic measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution function of a measurable map and layer-cake formula (Proposition 6.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given measurable f:X→[0,∞] on (X,ρ), define µ_f(E)=ρ({x: f(x)∈E}). Then for nonnegative Borel ϕ, ∫ ϕ(t) dµ_f(t) = ∫ ϕ(f(x)) dρ(x). In particular, integrals of functions of f can be computed from µ_f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by checking indicator functions, passing to simple functions, and then using monotone convergence. This yields the 'layer-cake' style identities used to relate distribution functions to L^p norms and other integral computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chebyshev inequality and relation of L^p norms to distribution function
rubrics_metrics.description: From the distribution function µ_f( (ξ,∞) ) = ρ({x: |f(x)|>ξ}) one obtains ∫ |f|^p dρ = ∫_0^∞ p ξ^{p-1} µ_f((ξ,∞)) dξ (layer-cake); in particular, µ_f((ξ,∞)) ≤ ξ^{-p} ∫ |f|^p dρ (Chebyshev's inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows how the tail behavior of µ_f controls integrability: if µ_f(ξ) were everywhere ≥ c ξ^{-p} the integral would diverge. Use Proposition 6.56 and monotone convergence to justify the formulas; Chebyshev's inequality is often used to bound measure of level sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone functions: only jump discontinuities and countability of jumps
rubrics_metrics.description: A monotone increasing function on R has left and right limits at every point; its only discontinuities are jumps, and there can be only countably many jump discontinuities on any bounded interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: if uncountably many jumps existed in a bounded interval there would be uncountably many of magnitude ≥1/n for some n, forcing unboundedness on a bounded interval. One can form F1(x)=lim_{t↓x} F(t) etc. Up to a countable set, a general monotone function differs from a right-continuous distribution function.
